one_liner: Nim event-loop library with a built-in HTTP/1.1 server that out-served Drogon by 1.34-1.39x in one the-benchmarker snapshot.
what_it_does: PowPow is a Nim networking library in the libuv/libevent role: an event loop with a timer wheel, plus TCP, UDP, TLS/DTLS, an HTTP/1.1 and experimental HTTP/2 server, WebSocket, a thread pool and file watching. The HTTP API is one callback, proc(req: HttpRequest, res: HttpResponse) {.gcsafe.}; there is no router, so you dispatch on method and path yourself or use the Supranim framework on top. newHttpServer(n) starts n worker threads, each with its own loop, sharing a port through SO_REUSEPORT.
how_it_is_fast: One edge-triggered epoll (kqueue on BSD/macOS) loop per worker thread, with SO_REUSEPORT spreading connections in the kernel, so workers never talk to each other. The HTTP/1.1 parser works on byte offsets and builds strings only on demand. CRLF and end-of-headers are found with SSE2 (scalar fallback elsewhere). Simple responses are built in one stack buffer and sent with a single send(), with the Date header cached. Connections, buffers, parsers, requests and responses come from pools, and writes are corked (TCP_CORK/TCP_NOPUSH) or batched with writev.
when_to_use: You write services in Nim and want one event-loop package that covers HTTP/1.1, WebSocket, TLS, UDP and raw TCP, not std/asynchttpserver.

Keep-alive HTTP/1.1 APIs with tiny responses on Linux, where you want most of the box's req/s from a few cores (in this table it served about 107-117k req/s per busy core, against about 70k for Drogon).
Prototyping or internal services where you control the clients and can accept a pre-1.0 library.
Zero-copy static file or media serving (sendfile, Range and conditional requests built in; optional kTLS and io_uring SPLICE paths).
when_not_to_use: Anything public-facing that needs a vetted server: the README says it is not production-ready and may contain bugs and security vulnerabilities, and a use-after-free in the event loop was fixed as recently as 2026-09-30.

If tail latency matters: in the same snapshot powpow's p99 was 7.6 / 15.9 / 21.3 ms at 64 / 256 / 512 connections, while cwist (C) was at 0.50 / 1.84 / 3.68 ms and agoo-c (C) at 1.18 / 7.7 / 11.5 ms (from data.json). The win is in throughput only.
If you need routing, middleware or a C/C++ API: it is a Nim library with a single callback, so it does not replace Drogon in a C++ codebase.
Multi-threaded serving on Windows: proto/multithread.nim compiles only when not defined(windows), and the README says it has been tested on Linux and macOS only.

If you need stable performance across releases: issue #2 (2026-08-04) records an 8x regression, from 138k/s to 16-30k/s, after security timer fixes. It was resolved, but it shows how sensitive the hot path is.

integration.dependencies: voodoo, nimsimd, mimedb, openparser, multipart, checksums (Nimble packages); OpenSSL 3.x for TLS
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll by default, io_uring opt-in with -d:powpowIoUring), macOS/BSD (kqueue), Windows (IOCP, single-threaded server only); SSE2 scanning on x86, scalar elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: One loop per worker thread with no shared state. Handlers must be {.gcsafe.}. Loop.stop() is safe to call across threads (eventfd or self-pipe). Thread-pool results come back as callbacks on one dispatch thread. The rate limiter was made thread-safe for multi-threaded mode (README security roadmap).

gotchas: Harness asymmetry in the suite build: nim/Dockerfile compiles every Nim entry with --passC:-flto --passL:-flto --assertions:off -d:release --opt:speed in the nimlang/nim:2.2 image (Debian bookworm). Drogon is built with plain cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release and no LTO on debian:trixie-slim. So the Nim side had LTO and the C++ side did not, and the two used different distro GCCs (inferred from the base images; versions not pinned). The record's 'no LTO' for powpow is wrong.

The suite flag -d:powpowPewPew is read only in powpow's own config.nims, where it turns on -d:danger, turns off bound and overflow checks and adds -march=native. The suite builds /usr/src/app/server.nim with powpow installed as a Nimble dependency. Nim reads config.nims only from the project directory and its parents, and the suite's nim/powpow folder has no config.nims (only config.yaml, server.nim and server.nimble). So the flag most likely did nothing in the published run, and no source file under src/ references it.

The suite entry was written by the powpow author. Until commit 4cce691 (2026-09-30) it ran one event loop (newHttpServer()), which explains the earlier single-core snapshots. The 2026-10-06 data.json is the only published run with the threaded server ahead of Drogon. That run was below the suite README's 75% server-bound threshold (powpow 53-56% CPU saturation, Drogon 62-63%), so the load generator may have been the ceiling.

Responses always carry Date and Connection headers but no Content-Type unless you set one. That is 99.3 bytes per response against Drogon's 78.3 in this suite, so powpow was not winning by sending less. README doc links point to docs/contents/..., but the repository ships md_docs/.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it if you work in Nim and want a full event-loop toolkit (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WS, TLS, UDP), not just a raw HTTP responder. In the same 2026-10-06 the-benchmarker table, jet_server (Dart) is 1.5-4% faster, while khttp and Tako (Rust) are 8-24% slower (derived from page data). The HttpArena entries (vanilla, zix, zeemo) carry stronger evidence because they beat a tuned nginx under one harness.
verified_claims_summary: In the independent the-benchmarker/web-frameworks suite (data.json, 2026-10-06; 3 trivial routes; 15 s runs at 64/256/512 keep-alive connections; each server in its own container with about 4 CPUs on a host reporting 'M1 Eight-Core Processor', 16 CPUs, Fedora x86_64 kernel), powpow 0.2 served 237,033 / 248,309 / 238,538 req/s. Drogon 1.9.13 (cmake release, no LTO) served 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358, so powpow was 1.34-1.39x faster. The two earlier snapshots, run before or just after the server was made multi-threaded, had powpow at 0.53-0.63x Drogon. powpow was built by Nim 2.2 with -O3-level speed options plus LTO.
status_note: Very active single-author MIT project (293 commits, latest 2026-10-06, version 0.2.2, 20 stars) that calls itself not production-ready; usable for Nim experiments and internal services, not as a hardened public server.
